name: Carla Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Carla, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company or party, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the wok and fryer section at Ondo, a small-plates place with an open kitchen, so the guests watch everything we do. I come in at three, set up my sauces and garnishes, and then from half five it's flames until eleven. At weekends I run my own dumpling stall at the market by the canal, which is my little side project.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the open kitchen, because people actually react when the wok flares up. What grinds me down is the same eight dishes every night with no say in the menu. That's partly why I do the stall, and I use an AI app every day to cost my dumplings, plan stock and write the little signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly, that's kind of how my AI app feels on a bad day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. At work I'd tell people it saves me an hour a week on the stall, which is real. Online I'd probably post my costing spreadsheet, because people always ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing big changes, and that's fine. I've got over a year of costs saved because I live with a flatmate and the stall makes a bit. Ondo's busy, and there are three other places on my street that would hire me tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wok station and grow the stall, maybe add a second day in the summer. I'd keep using the app for costing and signs, maybe try one that plans prep lists. In a year or two I'd look at a small lease for a dumpling counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A bit boring, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. If it stays a small helper, is that a let-down for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes, because I like toys. But the thing I care about is my own place. My own dumpling counter doesn't need a robot. It needs a lease and a good pork filling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that weighs on you in this picture, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent in the city keeps going up, and commercial leases are scary money. That's the real hurdle for my counter, not technology. I'd probably wait for a cheap spot near the market.

say: I'd say AI is **still useful**, just **not magic**.
I'd post my **costing spreadsheet** online, because people always ask.
think: Nothing big changes, and I've got **over a year** of costs saved.
Ondo's busy and **three places** on my street would hire me tomorrow.
do: Keep the **wok station** and add a second stall day in **summer**.
Look at a **small lease** for a dumpling counter in a year or two.
S0.quote: My own dumpling counter doesn't need a robot. It needs a lease and a good pork filling.
fieldNote: Carla already treats AI as a **daily tool** for her side business.
Her ambition is her own counter, and the obstacle is **commercial rent**.
Plenty of local jobs and strong savings make this picture **low stakes** for her.

steps.text: Add a second dumpling stall day at the canal market in summer
Keep the wok and fryer section at Ondo
Try an AI app that writes prep lists for the stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, now that's interesting. That's my kind of picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small cooks, because all the boring office stuff gets cheap. At work I'd show the others how I do my ordering with the app. Online I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's better for me than for Ondo. The kitchen keeps its cooks for a while, robots are slower, and I can run a small counter without paying a bookkeeper. My hands stay my job, and the thinking parts get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the lease for the dumpling counter sooner, maybe within a year, and use AI for ordering, bookings, accounts and the menu signs. I'd keep a few shifts at Ondo for the first six months as a safety net. I'd hire one other cook, which feels mad to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about the lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that do to the pop-up and to your plans for a counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pushes the counter forward. If the AI can do the books, the stock and the booking replies, I can run it lean. The difference between a dumpling counter that makes money and one that doesn't is two people instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ondo would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jae (her head chef) would hate it, because he still writes orders on a clipboard. And the woman who does our accounts two days a week might lose that work. I'd feel bad, but I'd still use the software.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for small cooks, because office work gets **cheap**.
I'd show the others at Ondo how I **order with AI**.
think: It's better for me than for Ondo, since my **hands stay my job**.
I could run a counter **without a bookkeeper**.
do: Sign the **dumpling counter lease** within about a year.
Keep a few **Ondo shifts** for six months as a safety net.
feel: **Excited**, with a little **nerves** about the lease.
S1.quote: The difference between a dumpling counter that makes money and one that doesn't is two people instead of three.
fieldNote: Carla reads this picture as an **opportunity**: cheap thinking work, safe hands-on work.
She openly admits the cost to **colleagues** but would still use the software.
Her nerves are about the **lease**, not about AI.

steps.text: Sign a lease for a small dumpling counter near the canal market
Run ordering, bookings and accounts for the counter with AI
Hire one cook to help on the dumpling counter
Keep a few Ondo shifts for the first six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oof. Two years. That's a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the cooks who own something will be okay and the ones on wages won't. That's harsh, and I'd probably say it more gently at work. Online I'd post about how to use the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my wok job at Ondo is gone around 2031, no question, because a robot that does the same eight dishes is exactly what they'd buy. The counter is the only plan that makes sense. But a counter run by one cook competes with a chain run by robots, and that's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the counter lease straight away, with a short two-year term so I'm not stuck. I'd put maybe half my savings in and keep the other half untouched. I'd use AI for everything that isn't cooking, and I'd start reading about cooking robots so I know when to buy one myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Thrilled and anxious at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have just opened your counter. What happens to it in 2031, when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the human part. People come to my dumpling stall to watch me fold dumplings and chat, and a robot can't do that. Or, if it can, I'd buy a robot for the frying and keep the folding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if things go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second cook goes first, which would be awful to tell them. Then my own pay. I'd never touch the untouched half of the savings, that's the rule.

say: I'd say cooks who **own something** will be okay and those **on wages** won't.
I'd post online about how to **use the gap**.
think: My **Ondo job** is gone around 2031, because robots suit eight repeat dishes.
A one-cook counter against **robot chains** is the only plan, and it's scary.
do: Sign a **two-year lease** straight away and invest half my savings.
Read up on **cooking robots** to know when to buy one for frying.
S2.quote: People come to my dumpling stall to watch me fold dumplings and chat, and a robot can't do that.
fieldNote: Carla expects to **lose her wage job** but has a business plan as her lifeboat.
She'd **automate** her own counter rather than fight robots.
Keeping **half her savings** untouched is her firm safety rule.

steps.text: Sign a two-year lease and put half the savings into the counter
Buy a frying robot for the counter once prices are known
Leave the Ondo wok station when the counter opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's actually enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window, so use it. At work I'd tell the younger cooks to start a stall, a pop-up, anything they own. I'd probably run a little talk at the market traders' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the picture where I come out best, I think. I'd open the counter, build regulars, and by 2034 I'd know exactly which jobs to give a robot. The thinking side, stock and books, would be AI from 2031 anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the counter within a year on a longer lease, because I'd have time to earn it back. I'd learn the AI tools for marketing, because that's my weak spot. I'd save part of the profits each month so I can afford a robot fryer around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change the counter plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm not sprinting. I'd test the menu at the stall first, then sign the lease. And I'd have regulars before the robots arrive, which matters most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd be fine. Is there a version of this where you're not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone loses their wages at once, nobody buys dumplings. That's the version where I'm not fine. A counter needs customers with jobs.

I'd tell young cooks to start **something they own**.
think: I'd have **regulars** and know which jobs to give a robot by **2034**.
The **stock and books** would be AI from 2031 anyway.
do: Open the counter within a year on a **longer lease**.
Save **part of profits** each month for a robot fryer around 2034.
S3.quote: If everyone loses their wages at once, nobody buys dumplings.
fieldNote: Carla sees **five years** as the ideal window to build a business.
Her real fear is **customers losing income**, not her own skills.
She'd put marketing, her **weak spot**, in AI's hands.

steps.text: Open the dumpling counter within a year on a five-year lease
Learn AI marketing tools for the counter's social media
Save part of monthly profits toward a robot fryer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is basically my whole thirties. Lots of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for being surprised. I'd say it nicely, but I'd say it. Online I'd share how I'm planning, because people like real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably have two counters by then. The AI would do the books from 2036 and robots would do frying by 2039, and I'd buy them as soon as they're cheap. I'm calm about it because I'd be the one buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the first counter in the next year, build it slowly and maybe open a second in five years. I'd keep using AI tools daily and keep a big cushion. Around 2036 I'd start shopping for kitchen robots properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, I'd take more time with the menu. Ten years means I can make mistakes and recover. Two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jae, your head chef, about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jae (her head chef) to start writing his recipes down, properly, because that's what will be worth money. Robots can cook, but someone has to decide what a good dish is. He's the best I know at that.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** for being surprised.
I'd share my **real numbers** online, because people like them.
think: I'd likely have **two counters** by the time robots arrive.
I'm calm because I'd be **the one buying** the robots.
do: Open the first counter next year and maybe a **second in five years**.
Start shopping for **kitchen robots** properly around **2036**.
S4.quote: Robots can cook, but someone has to decide what a good dish is.
fieldNote: With ten years, Carla sees herself as an **owner**, not a worker at risk.
She values **taste and judgement** as what stays human.
Her calm comes from **savings, adaptability** and a clear plan.

steps.text: Open the first dumpling counter next year and a second in five
Buy kitchen robots for the counters once prices drop
Keep using AI tools daily for stock, books and marketing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be opening a business in the middle of a storm. What would help is short, cheap leases for small food businesses and simple grants or loans for equipment. And honest numbers on robot prices, so small people can plan too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who eats the food. All of this only works if people still have money to spend on a nice dinner. A kitchen full of robots is pointless if the street outside is full of people who can't afford dumplings.

headlineQuote: A kitchen full of robots is pointless if the street outside is full of people who can't afford dumplings.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old wok cook** in an open-kitchen small-plates restaurant.
She runs a **weekend dumpling stall** and uses AI every day to cost and plan it.
She has over a year saved and sees her own **dumpling counter** as her future.
She treats AI and robots as tools she'd **buy herself**, staying calm in most pictures.
Her deepest worry is **customers losing their wages**, which would empty her counter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be opening a business in the middle of a **storm**.
whatWouldHelp: **Short, cheap leases** and simple equipment loans for small food businesses.
**Honest robot prices** so small owners can plan.
